where: Section 1, last paragraph of the cascode explanation
problem: The headroom cost is stated as 'Q1 needs VCE1 plus Q2's VBE, about 1 V extra'. The total minimum voltage from supply rail to output is indeed about 0.9–1 V (VCE1(sat) + VBE2), but the amount of extra headroom compared with a plain CE stage is only Q2's VBE, about 0.7 V. The word 'extra' with 'about 1 V' overstates the penalty and contradicts the table row that gives the cascode 0.7 V.
fix: Write: 'The price is headroom: the output can fall only to VCE1(sat) + VBE2, about 0.9 V, so the stage needs roughly 0.7 V more headroom than a plain CE stage.'

problem: The input pole is given as f = 1/(2π RsCM), as if the source resistance were the only resistance at the input node. The transistor's own rπ (and any base bias resistance) sits in parallel with Rs, so when Rs is large the formula overstates the pole frequency. The chapter itself says later that the input sees rπ of Q1.
fix: Write: f = 1/(2π(Rs ∥ rπ)CM), and add that when Rs is much smaller than rπ this reduces to 1/(2π RsCM).

problem: The caption says the upper chain 'stacks a common-emitter on a common-base stage', which reverses the physical order. In a cascode the common-base device Q2 sits on top of the common-emitter device Q1, as the lead and Section 1 correctly say.
fix: Write: 'The upper chain stacks a common-base stage on top of a common-emitter stage: the upper device shields the lower one's collector capacitance, so gain stays high while bandwidth widens.'

problem: The row puts two different quantities side by side. For the Darlington, 1.4 V is the input-to-output base-emitter drop of a buffer. For the cascode, 0.7 V is not an input-output offset at all; it is the extra DC headroom at the output (VBE of Q2). A student will read both as the same kind of offset.
fix: Rename the row 'Extra DC headroom / offset' and note that the cascode's 0.7 V is the extra voltage the output needs below the supply, while the Darlington's 1.4 V is the input-to-output base-emitter drop.
